clips.title: How I Review AI-Generated Code
clips.why: Owain Lewis explains why output that an AI wrote fast still needs a person's review, and what an AI review can and cannot replace. Our AI-drafted pages have exactly the same problem.
look: The problem he names with AI-generated work: it arrives fast and looks finished.
Why review still matters, and what changes when the author is a model.
Where he draws the line between an AI review and a human one.
clips.after: A brain page drafted by Claude Code is AI output too, so it starts at confidence: low and only its owner's review raises it.

clips.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADR) as a LOG that answers "WHY?"
clips.why: Derek Comartin explains what an architecture decision record is and why it is the place for the "why" that code cannot show.
look: The parts of a decision record he describes. Which of them do you find in ours: status, context, decision and consequences?
Why he calls it a log that answers "why?": the record stays when the people who decided have moved on.
clips.after: Our decision pages live in rnd-kb/decisions/ as ADR-NNNN-<slug>.md, starting with where the brain itself lives.

clips.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADR) as a LOG that answers "WHY?"
clips.why: A worked example of a real decision record, so you see how short and plain a good one is.
look: How short the example is: only what a reader later needs to understand the choice.
What the example records beyond the decision itself, and why a future reader needs it.
clips.after: When you write ADR-0002, one fresh VM per agent run, its consequences should name the costs too, such as a minute to start a run.

practice.q: Claude Code just drafted a page from its sources and nobody has checked it. What confidence does the frontmatter say?
practice.hint: The lowest of the three values.
practice.why: Every AI draft starts at low, so search, the index and the bot treat it as a lead until the owner checks it.

practice.q: Shai has drafted 18 engineering pages. How should they reach their owners?

options.text: One big pull request with all 18 pages, reviewed by Shai
options.why: Shai drafted them, so he is the wrong reviewer, and a reviewer handed 18 pages skims.

options.text: One pull request per owner, with only that owner's pages, and the owner as reviewer
options.why: Each owner reads only their own few pages, which is the only way they get read properly.

options.text: Merged straight away at low, because low already warns readers
options.why: Drafts do go through a pull request and lint, but the point of the review is to raise confidence, which only the owner can do.

practice.q: Which of these is a good seed page?

options.text: "How to write a Django view in fcp"
options.why: That is how to write code here, which the backend codebase skill already teaches.

options.text: "Why integration tests wait for the QA lock, and what to do", asked three times in public channels this quarter
options.why: Real, repeated demand, cross-team, and it explains how the system works and what to do.
Too big for one owner to check in one sitting. Big topics become several short pages.

practice.q: Put the life of a seed page in order.
items: The page goes into the seed plan with an owner who agreed and its sources
Claude Code drafts it from those sources, at confidence: low
The author deletes any claim the sources do not support and opens a pull request to the owner
The owner checks each claim against the code, fixes or deletes, and raises confidence
The page counts toward the 30 checked pages agents need
practice.why: Nothing counts for agents until a named owner has checked it, and the confidence and reviewed date record that check.

practice.q: A page's file says confidence: med, but it was reviewed 21 months ago with review_every: 90d. Does it count toward the 30?

options.text: Yes, because med or high counts
options.why: The count uses effective confidence, and this page is far more than twice overdue.

options.text: No, because it reads as low until its owner reviews it again
options.why: 21 months is far beyond 2 × 90 days, so every tool reads it as low.
Overdue is a lint warning, not an error, so lint passes either way. The count is what protects agents here.
